title: Alternating Current: Meaning, Characteristics and Reactance
summary: What alternating current is, its peak, rms, frequency and period, and how a resistor, inductor and capacitor behave in an a.c. circuit.

p: Alternating current (a.c.) is a current that reverses its direction regularly and changes continuously with time. Direct current (d.c.) flows in one direction only. An a.c. usually follows a sine wave: I = I₀ sin(ωt), where I₀ is the peak current, ω = 2πf is the angular frequency, f is the frequency in hertz and t is the time in seconds.

Frequency f: the number of cycles per second, in hertz (Hz). Period T: the time for one complete cycle, T = 1 ÷ f. Amplitude (peak value): the maximum value of the current or voltage. Root mean square (r.m.s.) value: the steady d.c. value that would give the same heating effect. I_rms = I₀ ÷ √2 (about 0.707 I₀) and V_rms = V₀ ÷ √2.
Example: the Nigerian mains supply is about 230 V (r.m.s.) at 50 Hz. Its peak voltage is 230 × √2 ≈ 325 V and its period is 1 ÷ 50 = 0.02 s.
Study the table.
A resistor (R): the voltage and current are in phase, and Ohm's law applies, V = IR.

An inductor (L): the current lags behind the voltage by 90°. Its opposition to the current is called inductive reactance, X_L = 2πfL, where L is the inductance in henry (H). It increases with frequency.

A capacitor (C): the current leads the voltage by 90°. Its opposition is the capacitive reactance, X_C = 1 ÷ (2πfC), where C is the capacitance in farad (F). It falls as the frequency rises. For a capacitor V = IX_C. (The lesson note writes V = IX_L here by mistake.)
Reactance and resistance are both measured in ohms.
ELI the ICE man: in an inductor (L) the e.m.f. (E) comes before the current (I), so current lags; in a capacitor (C) the current (I) comes before the e.m.f. (E), so current leads.

title: R-L, R-C and R-L-C Circuits: Impedance, Power and Resonance
summary: How the three components combine, impedance and phase angle, power and power factor, resonance and the resonant frequency.

p: A resistor and an inductor in series. The voltage leads the current. The impedance (the total opposition) is Z = √(R² + X_L²), and the phase angle is given by tan φ = X_L ÷ R.
A resistor and a capacitor in series. The current leads the voltage. Z = √(R² + X_C²), and tan φ = X_C ÷ R.
All three in series. The net reactance is X = X_L – X_C. The impedance is Z = √(R² + (X_L – X_C)²) and the phase angle tan φ = (X_L – X_C) ÷ R. The current is I = V ÷ Z.
Because X_L and X_C act in opposite directions, they partly cancel. The phasor diagram below shows this: reactances are drawn at right angles to the resistance, then added as vectors to get Z.

p: Phasors are rotating vectors that represent sinusoidal voltages and currents, and are used to show the phase relationship between them. In a pure R, V and I are in phase; in a pure L, V leads I by 90°; in a pure C, I leads V by 90°; in an R-L-C circuit the resultant is found by vector addition.

p: In a series R-L-C circuit, resonance occurs when X_L = X_C, that is, 2πfL = 1 ÷ 2πfC. At resonance the impedance is smallest (Z = R), the circuit behaves like a pure resistor, the current is largest, the voltage and current are in phase and the power factor is 1.
The resonant frequency is f₀ = 1 ÷ (2π√(LC)).

To see why, look at what happens as the frequency changes. For L = 1.0 H and C = 2.0 µF: at 50 Hz, X_L = 314 Ω and X_C = 1,592 Ω (so the capacitor dominates); at 112.5 Hz, X_L ≈ 707 Ω and X_C ≈ 707 Ω (they are equal: resonance); at 200 Hz, X_L = 1,257 Ω and X_C = 398 Ω (the inductor dominates). The lesson note's own picture was not suitable for reproduction (it mixed up the axes), so we give this table instead.

Power distribution on the grid (the national grid, once run by NEPA). Transformers (they work only with a.c.). Induction motors. Radio and TV tuners (they use resonance in R-L-C circuits to pick one station). Circuit breakers and relays. Household appliances such as fans and refrigerators. Signal processing in electronics.

title: Batteries: Cells, e.m.f., Internal Resistance and Safety
summary: What batteries are, primary and secondary types, how a cell works, e.m.f. versus terminal voltage, internal resistance, connecting cells, and safe use, with worked answers.

p: A battery is a device that changes chemical energy into electrical energy by electrochemical reactions between two electrodes in an electrolyte. A single unit is a cell; a battery is two or more cells joined in series or parallel to give a greater voltage or current.

Primary batteries cannot be recharged: the chemical reaction cannot be reversed. Examples: dry (Leclanché) cell, alkaline cell, mercury cell, zinc-carbon cell. Secondary batteries can be recharged: the reaction is reversible. Examples: lead-acid accumulator, nickel-cadmium, lithium-ion, nickel-metal hydride.

A cell has two electrodes (anode and cathode), an electrolyte (a solution or paste in which ions move), and an external circuit that gives a path for the electrons. Chemical reactions between the electrodes and the electrolyte free electrons at one electrode; they flow through the external circuit to the other electrode, giving an electric current.

The electromotive force (e.m.f., E) is the energy supplied by a source per unit charge in driving charge round the complete circuit, including inside the cell: E = W ÷ Q. Its unit is the volt. Terminal voltage V is the voltage measured across the terminals while the cell is supplying current: V = E – Ir, where I is the current and r the internal resistance. The 'lost volts' Ir is used up inside the cell.

A real cell is not a perfect voltage source: the materials inside have resistance r. It causes a voltage drop inside the cell when current flows, and the greater the internal resistance, the more energy is lost as heat. That is why a battery's voltage falls when it supplies a large current.

In series (positive of one to the negative of the next) the e.m.f.s add: E_total = E₁ + E₂ + … + Eₙ, and the internal resistances also add. In parallel (all positives together and all negatives together) the voltage stays the same (for identical cells) but the cells share the current, so the battery lasts longer and the internal resistance is smaller.

A battery of e.m.f. 12 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to a 5.5 Ω resistor. Total resistance = 5.5 + 0.5 = 6.0 Ω. Current I = E ÷ (R + r) = 12 ÷ 6.0 = 2.0 A. Terminal voltage V = E – Ir = 12 – 2.0 × 0.5 = 11 V.

Advantages: portable and compact; quiet and clean; useful in remote places; rechargeable types reduce waste; many sizes. Limits: limited capacity and life; pollution if wrongly thrown away; can leak or explode if abused; rechargeable batteries lose capacity with time; internal resistance reduces efficiency.
Uses: torches, phones and tablets, laptops, car batteries, storing solar energy, medical devices (such as pacemakers), remote controls, power banks and UPS units.

Do not mix old and new batteries. Do not short-circuit the terminals. Keep batteries away from heat and fire. Store them in a cool, dry place. Recycle dead batteries properly. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling lead-acid batteries. Never try to recharge a non-rechargeable cell.

sections.h: Extra detail: the dry cell and the accumulator
p: A Leclanché dry cell has a zinc case (the negative electrode), a carbon rod surrounded by manganese dioxide (the positive electrode) and an ammonium chloride paste as the electrolyte; it gives about 1.5 V. A lead-acid accumulator gives about 2 V per cell, so a 12 V car battery has six cells in series.

title: Solar Collectors: Types, Components and Comparison with Solar Panels
summary: How a solar collector turns sunlight into heat, its three main types, parts of a flat-plate collector and how it differs from a photovoltaic panel.

p: A solar collector is a device that absorbs sunlight and converts it into heat, which is used to heat a fluid such as water or air. It is part of solar thermal energy systems, as opposed to photovoltaic (PV) panels, which convert sunlight into electricity.

1. A dark surface (the absorber plate) absorbs sunlight. 2. Light energy changes to heat. 3. The heat passes to a working fluid (water, air or antifreeze). 4. The hot fluid is used directly or stored in an insulated tank.

Flat-plate collector: the most common type for homes; an insulated box with a transparent cover and a dark absorber plate; the fluid flows through tubes fixed to the plate. Evacuated-tube collector: parallel glass tubes with a vacuum between two layers to cut heat loss; works better in colder climates. Concentrating (parabolic) collector: mirrors or lenses focus sunlight onto a small area to reach high temperatures; used in industry and power plants.

title: Solar Collectors: Uses, Design for Efficiency and Calculations
summary: Advantages, limits and applications of solar collectors, passive and active systems, the design factors for efficiency and the heat-collected calculation.

p: A renewable source. Low running cost after installation. Friendly to the environment with no greenhouse gases made when running. Quiet. Good for rural and off-grid areas. Less dependence on fossil fuels. Simple upkeep and long life.

Depends on sunshine (less effective on cloudy and rainy days). The cost of installing it can be high. It needs space. Heat is lost at night if the storage is poor. It is not suitable for portable use. It may need antifreeze in cold climates (not an issue in Nigeria).

Heating water in homes; heating swimming pools; space heating; industrial process heating; solar desalination (making fresh water from sea water); heating greenhouses; solar cookers; solar drying of crops such as grain, cassava and pepper.

A passive system has no pump or controller. The water moves by natural circulation (thermosiphon): hot water is lighter and rises to the tank above, and cooler water sinks to the collector. It is simple, cheap and needs little maintenance. An active system uses pumps and controls to circulate the fluid; it is more efficient and suits larger or multi-storey buildings.

Tilt angle: roughly equal to the local latitude for the best absorption. Orientation: face the equator (south in the Northern Hemisphere, as in Nigeria; north in the Southern Hemisphere). Insulation: stops heat loss from the back and sides. Absorber material: a good conductor of heat such as copper or aluminium. Colour: black, to absorb the most radiation. Keep the cover clean and free of shade.

The useful heat power collected is approximately Q = A × S × η, where A is the area of the collector (m²), S is the solar intensity or insolation (W/m²) and η is the efficiency (usually 0.6 to 0.8). Q is a power in watts, not an amount of energy in joules; multiply by time to get energy.
Evaluation question 7: area 1.5 m², insolation 800 W/m², efficiency 65%. Q = 1.5 × 800 × 0.65 = 780 W. (The question calls it a 'solar panel', but because it asks for heat it is really a collector.)

sections.h: Care of a solar thermal system
p: Clean the cover regularly. Check pipes and joints for leaks. Check the insulation and the tank. Make sure no shade covers the collector. Drain or protect the system in freezing conditions (not usual in Nigeria). Have it checked by a technician once a year.

title: Second Term Revision: Fields, A.C., Batteries and Solar Collectors
summary: A checklist, formulas and the corrections made in the second term.

p: Electric field: definition, direction, E = F/q, E = kQ/r², Coulomb's law, field lines, uniform fields. Resistors: series and parallel. Magnetic field: sources, lines, rules, flux, F = BIL sin θ. Electromagnetic field: components, waves, Faraday's and Lenz's laws. A.C.: rms, reactance, impedance, power, resonance. Batteries: types, e.m.f., internal resistance. Solar collectors: types, parts, Q = ASη.

E = F/q; E = kQ/r²; F = kq₁q₂/r². R = R₁ + R₂ (series); 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ (parallel). Φ = BA cos θ; F = BIL sin θ; B = μ₀I/2R. I_rms = I₀/√2; X_L = 2πfL; X_C = 1/2πfC; Z = √(R² + (X_L – X_C)²); f₀ = 1/2π√(LC); P = VI cos φ. V = E – Ir. Q = ASη.

The field 0.1 m from 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C is 1.8 × 10⁶ N/C (not 10⁵). The field at the centre of a loop is μ₀I/2R. For a capacitor, V = IX_C (not X_L). X_L = 188.5 Ω gives Z = 195 Ω for the 0.5 H inductor. The unit of reactance is the ohm, not the farad. The solar collector gives heat power in watts.

Force between 6 µC and 8 µC at 3 m: 0.048 N. 0.5 m, 10 A, 0.3 T: 1.5 N. 2 m, 6 A, 0.5 T: 6 N. R-L-C with R = 10 Ω, X_L = 9 Ω, X_C = 4 Ω: Z = 11.2 Ω. f₀ for 1 H and 2 µF: 112.5 Hz. X_C of 100 µF at 50 Hz: 31.8 Ω. Battery example: 2 A and 11 V. Collector example: 780 W.
